props.title: No One's Crazy
lines: People are not dumb with money. They are consistent with their own history.
Your life is a tiny sample of the world, and a huge sample of your beliefs.

rows.v: Your personal money history may be 0.00000001% of what has happened in the world.
That same sliver may be about 80% of how you think the world works.
Equally smart people disagree on recessions, investing, priorities, and how much risk to take.
Frederick Lewis Allen: the Great Depression marked millions of Americans inwardly for life — with a range of experiences.
Asked what he remembered of the Depression, Kennedy said he had no first-hand memory of hardship — different life, different model.

props.title: November 2009 unemployment

left.name: The headline
lines: An average hides who actually lost work.

right.name: The split
lines: African American males age 16–19 without a high-school diploma: 49% unemployed.
Caucasian females over 45 with a college degree: 4% unemployed.
Local stock markets in Germany and Japan were wiped out in World War Two; German farms at war's end: about 1,000 calories a day.
The U.S. stock market more than doubled over the war years — not the same scar.

props.note: Figures as printed in the book for those dates.

props.title: A terrible product that still sells

rows.v: Lower-income households: about $412 a year on lottery tickets — four times higher-income households.
Those buyers are largely the same people who say they could not find $400 in an emergency.
As an investment the ticket is awful. As a purchased dream of a gap, it can be the only option in the room.
Do not call the buyer crazy until you see the financial room they live in.

props.title: Pensions were never universal

rows.v: End of 2018: about $27 trillion in U.S. retirement accounts.
Participation rate of men age 65+ stayed above 50% until the mid-twentieth century.
Ida May Fuller, 1940: first Social Security check $22.54 — about $416 in later dollars.
Average Social Security check for retirees did not exceed $1,000 a month, inflation-adjusted, until the 1980s.
More than a quarter of Americans over 65 were in Census poverty until the late 1960s.
Only a quarter of those 65+ had pension income in 1975; among them, ~15% of household income came from it.

props.note: Employee Benefit Research Institute, as cited in the book.

props.title: No one is crazy — they are local
items: People's money views are a product of when they were born, what they lived, and what they needed.
Do not expect a 1970s inflation scar and a 1990s bull-market childhood to produce the same investor.
A 'crazy' choice is often a rational answer to a room you have never stood in.
Your job is not to mock the lottery ticket. It is to notice that your own history is also a tiny sample.

props.title: Your sample is not the world
items: A Depression childhood and a 1990s bull-market childhood are different operating systems.
People buy lottery tickets for a story of control, not because they failed a probability class.
Respect the other room. Then notice that your own room is also small.
The chapter's mercy: nobody is crazy. They are local.
